column1: What does NoSQL stand for, and what class of system does it describe?
column2: Not Only SQL: a broad class of non-relational DBMS, often with a flexible schema, although some still use a table structure.

column1: Name the example system the lecture gives for each NoSQL type: graph, column-oriented, wide-column, in-memory, search engine, document.
column2: Neo4j, KDB, Cassandra, Redis, Elasticsearch, and MongoDB (covered in the next chapter).

column1: A graph fits in an edge table, so what is the problem with using an RDBMS for it?
column2: Joins are expensive, and discovering relationships between nodes requires a large number of joins.

column1: What is index-free adjacency?
column2: Storing pointers between connected nodes directly, which gives graph databases constant traversal time.

column1: How does breadth-first search explore a graph, and what is an example application?
column2: It explores all direct neighbours at depth 1 before moving to depth 2, and so on; for example, checking whether a user is within a certain distance of another user on a social network.

column1: What does PageRank measure, and what is an example application?
column2: The relative importance or influence of nodes in a network; for example, identifying key opinion leaders on social media.

column1: What are weakly connected components, as defined in the lecture?
column2: Subgraphs where every pair of nodes is reachable from one another; their number equals the number of islands.

column1: How is the graph built to detect someone operating hundreds of fake accounts?
column2: Each account is a node, and an edge joins two accounts sharing a value on one or more features (IP, credit card, Wi-Fi, delivery address); the fake accounts form a big weakly connected component.

column1: What three techniques reduce false positives in graph-based fraud detection?
column2: Filtering supernodes such as public computers, adding weights and a connectivity threshold, and only considering activities within a tight time window.

column1: How does community detection by label propagation work?
column2: Each node starts with a unique label and iteratively adopts the majority label among its immediate neighbours until convergence.

column1: What does the local clustering coefficient measure, and what is an example application?
column2: How close a node's immediate neighbours are to forming a complete graph; it is used in spam and fake account detection.

column1: What are the three components of an RDF record, and what is its query language?
column2: Subject, predicate and object; it is queried with SPARQL, the query language of the Semantic Web.

column1: What is the core difference between a standard RDBMS and a column-oriented database?
column2: An RDBMS stores data on disk by rows; a column-oriented database stores it by columns.

column1: With 3 values per disk I/O, why does summing one column of a 3-row, 4-column table take 3 I/Os in an RDBMS but 1 in a column store?
column2: The RDBMS has the column's values spread across the row-ordered data, whereas the column store keeps them together in one block.

column1: With 3 values per disk I/O, how many I/Os does inserting a 4-value record take in each storage layout?
column2: An RDBMS may need 2, while a column-oriented database needs 4, one for each column.

column1: Why can column-based storage achieve a higher compression rate?
column2: Data within the same column are of very similar nature; this lowers storage cost and speeds up processing.

column1: What does run-length encoding produce for `F, F, F, M, M, F, F`?
How does dictionary encoding compress a district column?
column2: It stores each distinct value as a small code plus a lookup, so Sha Tin, Central, Sha Tin, Tai Po becomes 1, 2, 1, 3 with the dictionary Sha Tin→1, Central→2, Tai Po→3.

column1: How do an RDBMS and a column-oriented database compare on reads and writes?
column2: An RDBMS is write-optimized; a column-oriented database is read-optimized, so more efficient for reads and less efficient for writes.

column1: What is the purpose of a wide-column database, and which system did the idea originate from?
column2: To be highly scalable through horizontal scaling; it originates from Google Bigtable (OSDI 2006), with Cassandra and HBase as examples.

column1: What is the Bigtable data model?
column2: A map `(row:string, column:string, time:int64) -> string`: given the row ID, column ID and timestamp, you get the data contents, so different versions can be retrieved.

column1: What is notable about the query language of Cassandra?
column2: CQL is SQL-like, but it has no JOIN operator.

column1: How does a Log-Structured Merge-tree handle writes?
column2: It buffers incoming writes in memory, occasionally flushes them to disk as immutable sorted records, and continuously merges and compacts them in the background, cleaning up deleted or outdated records.

column1: What are the advantages of a wide-column database?
column2: Massive horizontal scalability with the same underlying schema for all, fast write throughput from append-only mode (no locking), and no null overhead.

column1: What are the problems of a wide-column database?
column2: Poor support for queries needing joins, higher read latency than an RDBMS because of the effort to find the latest data in LSM trees, and only eventual consistency.

column1: Give the benchmark read/write speeds that motivate an in-memory database.
column2: Magnetic hard disk 80–160 MB/s, SSD 200–550 MB/s, RAM 2–20 GB/s.

column1: What querying limitations does Redis have as a key-value store?
column2: It indexes only the key, with no secondary index on other fields, so its querying power is limited.

column1: What are the two Redis persistence mechanisms?
column2: Snapshots of the dataset at specified intervals, and AOF, which logs every write so it can be replayed at startup; they can also be combined, or persistence turned off.

column1: Why is B-tree indexing unsuitable for an in-memory database, and what is preferred?
column2: B-trees are designed to be I/O optimal and are suboptimal in memory; a hash table is preferred, with $O(1)$ access but no range queries.

column1: What is NVRAM, and how could Redis use it?
column2: RAM that keeps data when the power is off but is slower than volatile RAM; it could serve as a faster layer for backup and recovery, not as primary memory.

column1: Give three use cases for an in-memory database.
column2: User session management, leaderboards in gaming, and high-frequency trading.

column1: What is the key component of Elasticsearch?
column2: An inverted index, which maps words to document IDs.

column1: What does each component of the Elastic Stack (ELK) do?
column2: Logstash is a data pipeline ingesting from multiple sources, Elasticsearch is the core engine, and Kibana is a frontend interface.

column1: List the stages of the text analysis pipeline in order.
column2: Character filter, tokenizer, normalization, stopword filter, stemming filter; a synonym filter can also replace or add tokens.

column1: What is the formula for TF-IDF, and how do the textbook and scikit-learn versions of TF differ?
column2: $\text{TF-IDF}(t,d)=\text{TF}(t,d)\times\text{IDF}(t)$. Textbook TF is the count of $t$ in $d$ divided by the total terms in $d$; scikit-learn TF is just the count.

column1: How do the textbook and scikit-learn versions of IDF differ?
column2: Textbook: $\log_{10}\left(\frac{N}{\text{df}(t)}\right)$. Scikit-learn: $\ln\left(\frac{N+1}{\text{df}(t)+1}\right)+1$.

column1: In the lecture's 3-document corpus, what is the scikit-learn IDF of "cat" (in all 3) and of "chased" (in 1)?
column2: $\ln(4/4)+1=1$ for "cat" and $\ln(4/2)+1=\ln(2)+1$ for "chased".

column1: What are the problems of TF-IDF?
column2: TF is counted linearly with no saturation, normalization is insufficient so longer documents are favoured, and there are no hyperparameters to tune.

column1: What two limitations of TF-IDF does BM25 address?
column2: Term frequency saturation, through a TF function capping how fast frequency raises the score, and length normalization, through tuneable parameters.

column1: What is fuzzy search in Elasticsearch?
column2: Returning results for similar words as well, with similarity measured by edit distance; it handles typos such as "box" for "fox".

column1: What does an embedding model do?
column2: It is a neural network mapping data (text, image or other types) to a dense vector, so that semantically similar inputs have close vectors.

column1: What are the steps of semantic search in a vector database?
column2: Chunk the text and embed each chunk into a vector, embed the query, then run a k nearest neighbour search for the closest data vectors.

column1: What are cosine similarity and cosine distance?
column2: Cosine similarity is $\frac{x\cdot y}{|x||y|}=\cos\theta$, with $\theta$ the angle between the vectors; cosine distance is $1$ minus the cosine similarity.

column1: When does cosine similarity reduce to a dot product?
column2: When the embedding model outputs unit vectors, because their magnitude is 1.

column1: How does the Inverted File Index (IVF) speed up kNN search?
column2: The data is clustered by K-means and the search narrows to candidate clusters; average $O(\sqrt{n})$, worst case $O(n)$, with approximate results.

column1: How are the layers of HNSW structured?
column2: Each higher layer is a sparser subset of the lower one, the ground layer contains all vectors, and each node keeps edges to its neighbours in each layer.

column1: How does an HNSW search proceed?
column2: From the top layer it greedily hops to the closest neighbours, then moves to a denser layer; at the ground layer it refines the closest neighbours and returns the top K.

column1: What is the advantage of IVF over HNSW, and of HNSW over IVF?
column2: IVF uses less memory; HNSW searches faster, $O(\lg n)$ against $O(\sqrt{n})$, and needs no re-training, whereas IVF requires K-means clustering.
